data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms not as an inductive inference of future truth, but as a non-inductive 'conventional decision' to act on the theory that has withstood the most severe attempts at falsification, thereby maximizing the potential for learning (verisimilitude) even if probability remains unchanged.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If verisimilitude cannot be coherently defined without invoking induction or probability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'conventional decision' to prefer corroborated theories implicitly assumes that past performance predicts future success (the very principle of induction Popper rejected).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory for practical purposes (e.g., building a bridge) logically entails a belief in its reliability that corroboration alone cannot justify.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Severity-Based Conventionalism: The rational agent adopts a rule (a convention) to prefer the theory that has survived the most stringent tests because this choice maximizes the growth of knowledge (closeness to truth/verisimilitude) should the theory be false, without assigning it a higher logical probability of being true. This separates the logic of testing (falsification) from the pragmatics of action (decision based on critical scrutiny).","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
